extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humor/travel literature; collectors or analysts of Mark Twain/19th-century travel satire
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Mark Twain's satirical travelogue Innocents Abroad that lampoons tourist behavior, expectations of pleasure excursions, and American travelers abroad; useful as an example of comic travel writing and social satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure-excursion expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any body's and every body's notion of a pleasure excursion is that the parties to it will of a necessity be young and giddy and somewhat boisterous. They will dance a good deal, sing a good deal, make love, but sermonize very little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the normative standard Twain cites for what a ‘pleasure excursion’ should be: youthful, lively, dancing/singing/romance, and minimal sermonizing. He contrasts this ideal with the reality aboard the Quaker City to produce comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-conducted-funeral characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any body's and every body's notion of a well conducted funeral is that there must be a hearse and a corpse, and chief mourners and mourners by courtesy, many old people, much solemnity, no levity, and a prayer and a sermon withal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain invokes this as the standard for solemnity and then humorously argues the voyage resembled a funeral more than a pleasure trip, underscoring mismatch between expectation and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: What the Quaker City excursion actually resembled
rubrics_metrics.description: “Three-fourths of the Quaker City's passengers were between forty and seventy years of age!... The venerable excursionists were not gay and frisky. ... They never romped, they talked but little, they never sang, save in the nightly prayer-meeting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific behavioral markers Twain lists to justify his claim that the trip was more like a ‘funeral excursion without a corpse’: advanced average age, abstention from common amusements, religiosity, and book-writing. Examples: limited dancing (three evenings, a single set), dominoes as the primary pastime, nightly devotionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominoes/croquet as neutral/insipid recreations (examples of shipboard leisure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The pilgrims played dominoes when too much Josephus or Robinson's Holy Land Researches, or book-writing, made recreation necessary -- for dominoes is about as mild and sinless a game as any in the world, perhaps, excepting always the ineffably insipid diversion they call croquet...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain uses these games as exemplars of the tame, decorous entertainments aboard — a criterion for the sort of genteel, unenergetic leisure that characterizes the voyage.

rubrics_metrics.name: American travelers’ conspicuousness and cultural conduct abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: “We always took care to make it understood that we were Americans--Americans!... We generally made them feel rather small, too, before we got done with them, because we bore down on them with America's greatness until we crushed them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A set of behavioral norms/anti-norms Twain attributes to his countrymen: loudness at table, haggling/squeezing value from money, conspicuous costume changes, and an imposition of national pride. He gives concrete anecdotes (bad French, costume incidents, fashion experiments) as guidance on how Americans made a sensation abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel writing valedictory should be complimentary but risks offending subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain describes his valedictory: “it is a proper, tolerably accurate, and exhaustive summing up of the cruise... If it is not a chapter that any company might be proud to have a body write about them, my judgment is fit for nothing.” Yet he reports passengers “took exceptions to the article.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit practical criterion for travel/press pieces: flattering, comprehensive summaries may still displease those praised; the writer should expect ingratitude and be cautious about generous public encomiums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotony of ship-life as a defining travel condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous diary-style entries and remarks: monotonous routine (services, dominoes, promenading, charades), the parody journal (“Monday--Got up, washed, went to bed.”), and statements like “It was a very comfortable prospect, though, for we were tired and needed a long rest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a criterion for the mood and tempo of long sea voyages in travel narrative: extended sameness, bouts of seasickness, limited variety in amusements — elements a travel writer can exploit for comic repetition or self-deprecating humor.
